title: Optimizer race (best-so-far vs evaluations): which converges faster at equal budget?
summary: The standard way to compare optimizers: the best objective value found so far, against the number of function evaluations, for several optimizers, each repeated many times, shown as a median line and a band over the repeats.

media.alt: Semi-log plot of best f so far against evaluations from 0 to 200 for three optimizers A, B and C: three falling lines with shaded bands, A lowest ending near 5e-3, B near 6e-2, C near 0.23.
media.caption: Reference render of class F7.1 (design-system gallery). The data are synthetic and exist only to demonstrate the form.

source.note: Plot class from the design system's plot taxonomy; synthetic demonstration data.

read_the_figure.question: Which converges faster at equal budget?
read_the_figure.data: best f vs n_eval per optimizer, repeats
read_the_figure.axes: x: number of function evaluations (0 to 200), linear. y: best objective value found so far, logarithmic (about 1.5e-3 to 1.2).
look_at: Which curve is lowest at the budget you care about, and by how many factors?
Do the bands of different optimizers overlap? Where do they separate?
How many evaluations does each optimizer need to reach a target value?
Is every optimizer given the same budget and the same repeats?
as_drawn: Three optimizers A (solid teal), B (dashed amber) and C (dash-dot blue), 15 repeats each. The lines are medians and each band is the minimum to maximum of the 15 runs.
All start at about 1. At 200 evaluations the medians are about 5e-3 (A), 6e-2 (B) and 0.23 (C): A is roughly 12 times lower than B and 45 times lower than C.
The bands are widest at the end (about one decade for A) and do not overlap between A and B or between B and C at 200 evaluations, but overlap earlier in the run.
The curves are smooth straight lines on the log axis, which is a property of the synthetic demonstration, not of real optimizers.
read_the_figure.proves: If the median of one optimizer is below the others and the bands are separated at the stated budget, that optimizer converged faster on this problem at this budget. It says nothing about other problems or other budgets.
if_wrong: Bands that overlap heavily: the difference is within run-to-run noise; add repeats.
Different budgets or different numbers of repeats per optimizer: not a fair race.
Linear y axis: the late progress, which spans decades, disappears.
must_check: median + band over repeats: one run is an anecdote; the median gives the typical path and the band the spread.
same budget: a race is only fair if every optimizer is stopped at the same number of evaluations.
log y: the interesting progress is over several decades, which a linear axis flattens.

terms.meaning: One call of the objective function; the usual unit of cost for an expensive problem.
The smallest objective value seen up to evaluation n; it never increases.
One independent run with a different random seed; stochastic optimizers need many.
The middle value over the repeats at each n, with the range (or a quantile interval) around it.
The maximum number of evaluations allowed.

remember: Best so far is non-increasing by construction.
On a log y axis a straight line is exponential convergence with slope -r.
Evaluations to a target: n(tau) = ln(f_0 / tau) / r.
Compare at equal budget and with equal repeats.
Report the median and a spread, not a single run.

understand.title: Marks and encodings
understand.text: Position on x is the evaluation count and on y the best value so far on a log scale. Each optimizer has its own colour and line style, so the plot works in greyscale; the line is the median and the shaded band of matching colour the range over the 15 repeats. The legend names the optimizers.

understand.title: Why this form answers the question
understand.text: Plain language: the question is who gets to a good answer first, for the same effort. Plotting the best value found against effort answers it at every budget at once. Repeating each run and showing a band tells you whether the gap is real or a lucky draw. The log axis lets you compare an optimizer that is at 0.1 with one at 0.001.

understand.title: How it misleads
understand.text: A band of the minimum to the maximum widens as repeats are added, so a bigger study looks noisier; a quantile band is steadier. Best-so-far hides how bad the typical current iterate is. Counting evaluations ignores the cost of the optimizer's own work. And a result on one test problem does not carry over: a race should be run on several, which is what F7.10 summarises.

understand.title: Alternatives
understand.text: The fraction of runs that reach a target value against evaluations (a data profile or empirical cumulative distribution of run lengths) answers the question 'how often does it succeed in time' directly. A rank plot across test problems (F7.10) summarises many problems. A table of evaluations to reach a target, with a median and a quantile range, is compact.

understand.title: A variant to create
understand.text: Draw the 25th to 75th percentile band instead of the range, add a horizontal dotted line at your target value and a vertical tick where each median crosses it, and add a fourth optimizer to see where the bands start to overlap.

steps.title: Best so far and its rate
steps.note: On the log axis a straight line has slope -r; the speed of an optimizer is r.

steps.title: Evaluations to reach a target
steps.note: For a target of 0.1 and rates 0.03, 0.015 and 0.008 per evaluation this gives about 77, 154 and 289: the third exceeds the budget of 200.

steps.title: Ratio of speeds
steps.note: A needs half as many evaluations as B for any target: the ratio of the rates 0.03 and 0.015.

worked.title: Reading the race from the reference render
worked.problem: (1) What are the three medians at 200 evaluations and what are the ratios? (2) About how many evaluations does each optimizer need to reach 0.1? (3) Is the difference between A and B at 200 evaluations larger than the run-to-run spread?

solution.text: (1) Read the lines at the right edge: about 5e-3, 6e-2 and 0.23.
(2) Follow the 0.1 level: A reaches it near 85 evaluations, B near 165 and C does not within 200. The straight-line model gives 77, 154 and 289.
(3) At 200 evaluations the top of A's band is about 2e-2 and the bottom of B's band is about 3.5e-2, so the bands are separated: the difference exceeds the spread of the 15 runs.

worked.answer: Medians of about 5e-3, 6e-2 and 0.23 (ratios 12 and 46); about 85 and 165 evaluations to reach 0.1 for A and B, never for C; at 200 evaluations the bands of A and B do not overlap.

analyze.q: Why can the median of B lie outside the band of A in some places but not others?
analyze.hint: Look at where the bands overlap.

analyze.q: What would the plot look like if A were only lucky in one seed?
A new optimizer is tested with only 3 repeats. How would you present the result?

evaluate.q: A is fastest in this figure. Do you recommend it for your problem?
evaluate.hint: Other problems, other budgets, tuning effort.

create: Redraw with a 25-75 percent band and a dotted target line with the crossing points marked.
Draw the fraction of runs reaching a target of 0.1 as a function of evaluations for each optimizer.

checks.q: Why is a band over repeats necessary?
checks.hint: What does one run tell you about the next?
checks.answer: Stochastic optimizers give different results each run; the band shows whether a gap between optimizers is larger than that variation.

checks.q: A median curve drops from 1 to 0.01 over 100 evaluations. What is its rate and how many evaluations to reach 0.1?
Two optimizers have bands that overlap by half at the budget. What can you say?
checks.answer: Not that one is better: the difference is within the run-to-run spread. Add repeats, use a quantile band or a rank test, or look at other budgets.
